posts.title: Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker
You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years.
For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run. This post is about them, and about single-tenant Titus, a mode that gives a task its own virtual machine while keeping everything else about Titus the same: the API, the deployment path, and the managed experience where the Compute/Platform team, not the application team, owns the host.
We will walk through why shared-kernel isolation runs out of road for certain workloads, how we measure isolation rather than asserting it, the options we weighed (microVMs, gVisor, EC2, and more shared-kernel tuning) and why a dedicated VM inside Titus won, how the mode is built on the Titus federation layer and autoscaling, and what we have seen along three axes: isolation, fleet efficiency, and the operational cost of keeping the fleet patched.
The cost of good neighbors
Multi-tenancy is a tradeoff. Packing many containers onto a large bare-metal instance keeps utilization high, but it also means those containers share a single Linux kernel and the underlying hardware. Titus isolates them with the tools the kernel provides: cgroups cap CPU, memory, and disk; namespaces give each container its own view of the system; seccomp and AppArmor restrict the system calls a container can make; the Completely Fair Scheduler divides CPU time; the iocost controller meters disk IO; and traffic shaping meters each container’s slice of the network. Each container also gets its own identity, IAM role, and security groups, so tenants are isolated for security and resource management.
These mechanisms provide isolation for what the kernel can partition. They cannot fully partition what is shared in hardware. A group of cores shares a last-level cache and a path to memory, so a container that suddenly pulls a lot of data from RAM evicts a neighbor’s cache lines and slows it down, even when both stay inside their CPU limits. There is no cgroup for memory bandwidth or cache residency, as there is for CPU shares. The interference is real, it is hardware, and it does not show up as either container exceeding its quota.

A noisy neighbor and a co-located app each stay within their cgroup CPU and memory limits, but both draw on a shared last-level cache and memory bandwidth that lack cgroup fences. The noisy neighbor takes most of it, so the co-located app stalls and its tail latency rises even though no one exceeded a quota.
We have written about this before. Predictive CPU isolation of containers at Netflix moved some placement decisions out of the kernel and into a service that forecasts each container’s CPU demand and re-pins containers to cores to reduce cache interference, formulated as a combinatorial optimization solved every minute. Noisy Neighbor Detection with eBPF instruments the kernel scheduler to surface per-container run-queue latency, so we can see a victim being starved in close to real time. And Mount Mayhem traced container-startup slowness to a global kernel lock amplified by modern CPU cache topology. Each of these raised the floor for everyone on the platform, and we are continuing that work.
A decade of shared-kernel isolation, at Netflix and across the industry, has not made co-tenancy invisible, because a noisy neighbor is not one problem but a family of them. Almost every physical resource a host shares is its own axis of interference, and a cgroup can fence very few of them:

CPU performance indeterminacy. Co-located threads contend for the run queue, so scheduling latency rises even while a container remains within its CPU quota. Separately, a neighbor with a large working set evicts a tenant’s last-level cache lines and saturates memory bandwidth, neither of which a CPU share can partition.
Network bandwidth and packets per second. Per-container shaping competes for link bandwidth, and receives processing runs in softirq context, charging one container’s packet work to whatever CPU a neighbor is running on. A flood of small packets exhausts a core’s softirq budget long before any bandwidth cap is reached.
Storage bandwidth and IOPS. A neighbor saturating a device’s queue serializes everyone’s I/O, and on cloud block storage, the per-volume and per-instance throughput ceilings are a shared budget in their own right.
Long tail. Page-cache reclaim, NUMA and cross-socket interconnect traffic, TLB-shootdown interrupts, PCIe and GPU contention, package-level power and thermal throttling, and contention on kernel global locks (the class of problem behind Mount Mayhem) each degrade neighbors in their own way.

What unites them is that they are physical, shared, and below the level a quota can reach. A platform can cap how much CPU time or memory a container is granted; it cannot hand each tenant its own slice of the memory bus, its own softirq budget, or its own portion of the last-level cache.
Of these, the network dimension has bitten hardest in our experience. Per-container bandwidth shaping uses a hierarchical token bucket (HTB) queueing discipline that serializes traffic with a global lock to account for each container’s bytes and packets. Under a flood of small packets from a single container, contention for that lock can burn kernel CPU and starve co-located containers of the time they need to process their own traffic, resulting in TCP retransmits and tail-latency spikes on services that did nothing wrong. The mechanism meant to prevent noisy neighbors becomes one.
The workloads most exposed to this are stateful, high-throughput streaming jobs: real-time data pipelines and stream processors that continuously move large volumes of data and maintain in-memory state. When one of these is perturbed, recovery is not cheap. A stream processor that falls behind or loses its place may have to restore from a checkpoint and pause processing for many minutes to catch up. For these jobs, intermittent interference from a neighbor is not a small slowdown that averages out; it is a stop-the-world event that pages an on-call engineer. The same teams report, accurately, that they never saw this on a plain EC2 instance.
Why we kept coming back to the VM
Full VM isolation, where a workload gets its own host and kernel, is the standard our customers are already happy with. The question was not whether VM isolation works; it was how to offer it without giving up what makes Titus worth using. We weighed four paths.

Keep improving shared-kernel isolation. This helps every workload on the platform, needs no opt-in, and we are still investing in it (more on the roadmap below). Its limitation is structural. Each round of tuning narrows the gap without closing it, because the underlying hardware remains shared. Cache, memory bandwidth, and the kernel’s own shaping and scheduling locks are not things a container boundary can fully contain. Shared-kernel isolation is the right default and the wrong promise for a workload that cannot tolerate a bad minute.
microVMs (Firecracker, Kata Containers). Lightweight VMs boot in about 150 milliseconds by emulating far less hardware than traditional VMs, which is why they power serverless platforms. They were the most appealing alternative on paper, and we carefully reviewed them. Three things made the cost hard to justify. First, the hardware virtualization they rely on is available only on bare-metal instances or through nested virtualization, and nested virtualization was not ready on the instance types we run at Netflix at the time, so adopting microVMs broadly would have constrained us to a narrow slice of the fleet. Second, there is no managed microVM service we could build on, which means we would have to run and maintain a virtualization layer ourselves: patching the hypervisor, live-migrating guests, and qualifying emulated devices. That is exactly the kind of operational surface we prefer not to own when we can avoid it. Third, even setting those aside, microVMs add virtualization overhead on CPU- and IO-bound work and do not support GPUs. Excellent isolation, but at a price in flexibility and operational load we were not willing to pay.
gVisor. A user-space kernel that intercepts system calls provides sandbox-grade isolation without a hypervisor, thereby avoiding the bare-metal constraint. The catch is performance and dependency. Intercepting syscalls in user space adds overhead on IO-heavy paths, which are precisely the workloads we most need to protect, and the open-source project lags behind its internal counterpart in fixes and is effectively maintained by a single vendor. The isolation we would gain came with a throughput tax on the exact jobs we were trying to help.
Move the workload to EC2. It is possible to run containers directly on EC2 instances. The problem is that the application team takes back the operational load that Titus exists to carry: choosing instance types, patching hosts, and sizing and scaling the fleet. For a team that came to Titus precisely to avoid those things, this is a regression in the experience, and the move between Titus and EC2 has historically been a one-way door that teams are reluctant to cross.

Spectrum of isolation options from lighter and more shared to stronger isolation: shared-kernel containers, then gVisor, then microVMs (Firecracker or Kata), then a full VM as used by single-tenant Titus, which is highlighted. Each option is annotated with its launch latency, overhead, and the entity that operates it; single-tenant Titus is a dedicated EC2 instance with no additional virtualization overhead.
There is also a question of what kind of isolation we actually need. microVMs and gVisor are built for security isolation between mutually distrusting tenants, the case where one tenant might actively try to attack or escape into another. Among Netflix teams, that threat model is more than the situation warrants. What these workloads need is resource and performance isolation: a guarantee that a neighbor cannot steal their CPU, cache, memory bandwidth, or network, not protection from a hostile co-tenant. A dedicated EC2 VM delivers exactly that, with hardware we do not have to emulate and a kernel we do not have to sandbox. We pay for the isolation we need rather than for a stronger security boundary.
microVMs and gVisor asked for a large, bespoke investment with real risk in order to approximate something we could get directly: a VM. Using EC2 to run containers provides the VM, but takes away the managed experience. So we took the direct route and brought single-tenant VM isolation into Titus itself, under the existing API and the existing shared-responsibility model.
How single-tenant Titus works
The idea is simple to state: a single-tenant task runs on its own EC2 instance, sized to fit it, with nothing else scheduled alongside. That instance is still a Titus container host that the Compute/Platform team owns and patches. The team running the workload sees the same Titus API and the same deployment path. Nothing about how they package or ship the job changes.

Side-by-side anatomy of a multi-tenant Titus, where multiple teams’ containers share one Linux kernel and the hardware beneath it and contend with one another, versus a single-tenant node where one task plus its platform sidecars owns the whole machine with no co-tenants.
Most of the work happens in the federation layer, the part of Titus that decides where a job runs (which cell, which capacity) before it is scheduled onto a node.

When a job is eligible for single tenancy, three things happen.

Federation decides eligibility and the envelope. Eligibility is governed by an allowlist maintained by the Compute/Platform team; a team opts in by targeting a single-tenant workload group rather than flipping a flag in the public API. For an eligible task, federation tags it as single-tenant and records the set of instance families it may run on, ensuring consistent performance across the workload. Consolidating this decision in federation follows the same principle we use for routing in general: placement intelligence belongs in one place, above the individual cells, where it can account for capacity and availability across the region.
Autoscaling provisions a dedicated node. Given a pending single-tenant task, our autoscaling implementation launches the smallest instance that satisfies the task’s requested CPU, memory, and GPU from the allowed families for the task just in time. Taking the tightest fit keeps the unused remainder of each dedicated node small. The next section covers this in detail.
The scheduler enforces one task per node. Single-tenant pods are configured with pod anti-affinity to prevent colocation with other pods, along with a priority class that exempts the task from preemption. Single-tenant nodes are also tainted to prevent unrelated workloads from being placed there, with only single-tenant workloads tolerating this taint. We also disable defragmentation/repacking for these nodes, so a single-tenant task is never relocated to repack the fleet. Together, these mean a single-tenant task has its host to itself for its entire life, undisturbed by a neighbor or by the platform’s own bin-packing.

Two design choices are worth dwelling on. First, single tenancy is allowlisted on purpose. If it were a free checkbox in the API, most teams would tick it, because who wouldn’t want a quieter host? And the efficiency that multi-tenancy exists to provide would erode across the fleet. Keeping the Compute/Platform team in control lets us direct dedicated isolation to workloads that need it and steer the rest toward shared capacity, while keeping the public API surface small as we learn. Second, we do not silently resize anyone’s job to fill its node. The job keeps the resources it requested; we recommend sizing it close to a node shape so the dedicated instance is well utilized, while keeping the workload portable and running identically whether in single-tenant mode or not, regardless of the host’s dimensions. Moving in and out of the mode is a configuration change, not a rewrite.
A few perpetrators, a lot of collateral damage
Noisy-neighbor pain is not spread evenly. In practice, a small number of workloads cause most of the disruption: a job that floods the host with small packets, churns the page cache, or saturates memory bandwidth degrades the performance of every other container unlucky enough to share its host. Some of these are also among the workloads most affected by contention, because a job can be both a source of interference and sensitive to it. The shape of the problem is a few perpetrators and many victims.
That shape is what makes single tenancy a precise lever rather than a blunt one. We do not need to give every workload its own machine. We need to pull the handful of perpetrators and the most disruption-sensitive victims onto dedicated nodes. Doing so protects their former neighbors directly and removes the reason the platform was spreading sensitive workloads apart with anti-affinity placement in the first place. The hosts left behind are quieter, and because they no longer have to be kept partly empty to honor spread rules, they pack more densely.

Before-and-after view of the Titus fleet. Before: a few red perpetrators are scattered across shared hosts, the amber workloads beside them are disrupted, and anti-affinity spreading leaves dashed stranded capacity. After: each perpetrator runs on its own dedicated single-tenant node, the remaining shared hosts are fully loaded with healthy workloads, and one host’s worth of capacity is reclaimed.
On the left is the fleet before: perpetrators sit on shared hosts, the workloads next to them suffer, and anti-affinity rules leave gaps that cannot be filled. On the right is the same fleet after: each perpetrator has its own right-sized node where it can be as noisy as it likes, with no one to disturb; the remaining hosts run full of undisturbed workloads; and the capacity that used to be stranded comes back. A few dedicated nodes buy isolation for the perpetrators and a calmer, denser fleet for everyone else.
Provisioning many small nodes
Single tenancy trades fewer large, shared instances for more small, dedicated ones, and that shift has consequences across the stack.
The first is the control-plane load. More nodes mean more for the Titus control plane to track and more VM launches against the EC2 control plane, the latter mattering most during a regional failover, when we scale up the fastest and can least afford a throttle. Titus is already a federated system: each region is divided into independent cells, which limit how large any single control plane can get, and let us add capacity by adding cells rather than growing a single stack without limit. We migrate workloads in stages rather than all at once, and we exercise the launch-rate path under controlled load on a schedule rather than discovering its limits during an incident.
The second consequence is capacity management, where the design changed the most. With one task per node, the fleet now spans many instance shapes whose demand shifts continuously as jobs come and go. Pre-staging static pools of every shape would be slow to manage and wasteful, so we instead provision single-tenant nodes on demand. It handles provisioning end-to-end, and several of its features line up with exactly what single tenancy needs:

Just-in-time, right-sized provisioning. Single-tenant jobs are configured with a list of supported instance families based on their performance requirements. At launch, they are mapped to the best-fit node size by comparing requested resources against the selected instance families. New nodes of that instance type are brought up by the autoscaler to meet the pending demand. Single-tenant pods are configured with anti-affinity to all other pods, so the scheduler naturally lands one pod per autoscaled node. Newly vacated nodes may be reused by any pending deploys before they’re automatically torn down. The node pools themselves are shared across single-tenant workloads and describe a catalog of available instance families and sizes.
Single tenant node pools. Single tenant may run in separate clusters or be shared with multitenant clusters. The pools are configured with a list of supported instance-type permutations and are pinned to a Titus container host AMI. This is where the managed experience lives: the host image and its configuration are ours, declared once and applied to every node created.
Consolidation management. In multi-tenant environments, we default to a repack/defrag behavior that periodically relocates workloads. This doesn’t apply in single tenant, where nodes are explicitly each running at most one workload. We therefore reclaim only nodes vacated by workloads that have scaled in or terminated. Node termination is performed in two stages, allowing nodes to be reused for pending workloads before they are fully terminated.
Drift-based patching. When we publish a new container host AMI, we support a “mutable” deploy to existing nodes without affecting any hosted containers, and an “immutable” deploy that updates the target AMI for newly created nodes. This means that many node upgrades don’t require disrupting workloads, but we reserve the right to roll the fleet with our users if needed.

The launch-latency tax, and why warm pools are harder here
Provisioning on demand does not make a node appear instantly, and launch latency is the tradeoff single tenancy asks us to manage most carefully. Bringing a single-tenant task to the point where it can serve traffic has two parts: standing the node up (booting a fresh EC2 instance, then pulling and extracting the container image, which is the largest part of host setup for most jobs) and the application’s own startup (a JVM loading and JIT-compiling its classes, a cache filling, and so on). A fresh instance takes tens of seconds before the image pull even begins.
In multi-tenant Titus, most of this is hidden. A new task usually lands on a Titus container host that is already running and already has the image layers cached, so starting it takes only a few seconds rather than minutes; the host boot was paid for once, long ago, and amortized across every task that has run there since. Single tenancy gives up that hiding place. Every single-tenant task waits for its own machine to boot and pull its image.
The usual remedy is a warm pool: keep some instances booted and idle so a pending task lands on one immediately. This works well for the multi-tenant fleet precisely because that fleet is close to homogeneous. A handful of large shapes cover almost everything, since any task can be packed onto a big shared host. A small amount of warm capacity in a few shapes gives a high hit rate, and its cost is spread across the many tasks that will use it.
Single tenancy inverts those economics, and this is the part worth being explicit about.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Because every task gets a right-sized node, the fleet spans many instance shapes (several families across many sizes), and a warm instance only helps a pending task whose shape matches it. A warm r7i.2xlarge does nothing for a task that needs an m7a.8xlarge. To achieve a good hit rate, we would need to hold idle capacity in every family-and-size bucket, and idle capacity in a bucket with no task to fill is pure cost. The very property that makes single tenancy efficient at steady state, tight best-fit sizing, works against warm-pool reuse: more distinct shapes mean more buckets and a lower hit rate per dollar of standing capacity. And the pressure peaks exactly when it is least welcome. During a regional failover or a live event, when many tasks need fresh nodes at once, a thin warm pool spread across many shapes drains immediately, and the rest of the demand pays the full cold-boot cost.
So we treat warm capacity as a small, targeted lever rather than a default. We keep a little pre-warmed capacity for the most latency-sensitive single-tenant starts, and we deliberately narrow the menu of shapes to a curated set of sizes rather than the full continuum, so warm capacity concentrates into fewer buckets and trades a little best-fit efficiency for a better hit rate. Everything else provisions just-in-time and accepts the boot.
The more durable wins are in cutting the launch cost itself rather than pre-paying for it, and they help both single- and multi-tenant nodes, which is the better place to spend the effort:

Faster image distribution. The image pull dominates the host setup, so newer OCI image formats and lazy-pulling snapshotters such as stargz and SOCI, which fetch only the bytes a container actually reads at startup rather than the whole image up front, reduce the largest component of the gap.
Checkpoint and restore. For processes that are slow to initialize, snapshotting a warmed-up application with a tool like CRIU and restoring it, rather than cold-starting it, removes most of the second half of launch latency.
Instance type selection. In multitenant configurations, we have historically used metal instances, which offer slightly better performance but come with a slower startup time. In a single-tenant configuration, node startup latency is more important, so we have moved away from these instances.
Scheduling optimization. Through regular stress testing of fleet scaling, we found a scheduling bottleneck caused by Kubernetes preemption logic, leading to nodes being scaled up quickly but then left idle while waiting for workloads to be scheduled on them. This was ultimately unnecessary, as our single-tenant pools do not run preemptible workloads. Disabling preemption greatly improved scheduling performance when under strain.

None of this makes the tradeoff disappear, and it is worth stating plainly: a single-tenant node is slower to stand up than a slot on an already-warm shared host, and hiding that with warm pools costs more per node here than it does on the multi-tenant fleet, because the warm pool cannot be as homogeneous. But for the long-running services that single tenancy targets, paying that cost once at launch in exchange for a quiet life afterward is a trade these teams are glad to make.
Measuring the difference
Isolation claims are easy to assert and hard to trust, so we measure them with a repeatable benchmark and a single score.
The method is a differential one. We run a reference container, a healthy and representative application, and record its throughput and tail latency while it runs alone. Then we run it again next to a havoc container engineered to be a bad neighbor: a UDP flood through XDP to stress the network-shaping path, pointer-chasing and STREAM to pollute the last-level cache and saturate memory bandwidth, fsync storms against the disk, stress-ng to abuse the scheduler, and GPU-burn to monopolize an accelerator. We only trust a run once the host has reached a steady state, which we confirm with the kernel’s Pressure Stall Information: we wait until cpu_some or mem_some shows that tasks are actually stalling on a contended resource, not merely that the resource is busy. Each scenario is run many times with fixed seeds, and we report the median with a bootstrapped confidence interval, because noisy-neighbor distributions are heavy-tailed and a simple average can mask the spikes that matter.
From the reference container’s numbers, we derive a simple measure of how well isolation held. Throughput efficiency is the fraction of operations per second the app retains under attack; latency efficiency is the ratio of its undisturbed P99 to its P99 under pressure. A neighbor that doubles the reference app’s P99 drops the latency efficiency. As an illustration, a reference app whose P99 latency goes down next to a havoc container achieves a certain latency efficiency, and one whose throughput falls from a to b operations per second achieves a certain throughput efficiency. The composite score is a weighted blend of the two, with a latency-sensitive preset that gives greater weight to tail latency for interactive and streaming-path services. A perfectly isolated system scores 100%, and a single hard failure invalidates the run regardless of the average.
Noisy-neighbor isolation
cgroups container isolation isn’t perfect, and applications may experience worse performance due to sharing a machine with a determined neighbor. This could extend to disk and/or network IO where the same volumes or interfaces may be shared across workloads. For a distributed workload, this can lead to measurable inconsistencies in performance depending on where the replicas are placed. For more sensitive workloads, this variance can mean the difference between stability and getting paged.
The single-tenant option makes it possible to better isolate workloads that cause problems for their neighbors and/or are more sensitive to such problems. This can be used as a stopgap until the specific regression problem is resolved and consistency is restored, or kept permanent for load patterns that aren’t worth supporting in a shared environment.
Efficiency
The second effect is fleet efficiency, and it is the one people expect to go the wrong way. Dedicating a node to a single task consumes that node’s slack, so the naive expectation is that utilization falls. In aggregate, it can move the other way, for a reason related to how we dealt with poor isolation before single tenancy existed.
To protect sensitive workloads on shared hosts, the platform used anti-affinity placement, scattering them across the fleet to reduce colocation of the same workload on the same nodes. Spreading fights bin-packing: it strains capacity, because a host kept partly empty to honor an anti-affinity rule cannot be filled by a workload that would otherwise have fit there. When isolation-sensitive workloads move to dedicated nodes, the need for spreading and fragmentation goes away, and the remaining multi-tenant fleet can pack more densely.
Another source of fragmentation is services that are sensitive to disruption. These are typically stateful services where recovery is expensive. As these services become more common in a given population, they can lead to nodes being held up by pods with strict disruption requirements. This can lead to an inability to defrag and recompact the pool during off-peak times. The symptoms and resulting drop in fleet efficiency caused by disruption-sensitive workloads mirror what’s observed for workloads with anti-affinity rules.
Depending on the magnitude of the anti-affinity and/or disruption budget problem, moving such workloads to single-tenant pools can result in equivalent or even improved placement when all costs have been accounted for. It also becomes easier to quantify the cost to end-users. Rather than trying to attribute fleet-wide fragmentation to individual workloads, we can directly quantify waste as single-tenant node overhead.
The theory and the practice diverge here, and it was the practice that decided it. In principle, the efficiency ceiling is higher for multi-tenant bin-packing: pack enough tasks together, and a host fills almost completely. We do not reach that ceiling. AWS offers a discrete set of instance sizes, so a large shared host rarely matches the exact sum of the requests we place on it, and the gap between a host’s capacity and what we can actually pack onto it is a bin-packing hole we cannot fill. At the granularity of large instances, those holes are sizable. Right-sizing an instance to a single workload, picking the closest fit from many shapes instead of draping many workloads over one big host, captured more of the available efficiency in our experience than the higher theoretical ceiling ever delivered. The clean theory favored multi-tenancy; our measured fleet favored right-sizing.
Container-host maintenance
The third effect is operational, and it shows up in how we keep the fleet patched. A multi-tenant host is hard to take down for maintenance precisely because it is full: draining it means relocating many tenants at once, several of which carry disruption budgets that limit how fast they can move, so a routine patch becomes a careful, coordinated evacuation. A single-tenant host runs exactly one task, with consolidation and defragmentation turned off, so draining it means relocating only the one workload, and we can automatically handle that when a new AMI ships. The remaining multi-tenant hosts are easier to maintain, too, because the workloads that were most sensitive to disruption are no longer stranded on them.
What it changes, and what it doesn’t
Single-tenant mode is a configuration, not a migration. A team moves a workload onto a dedicated node, and back, with a labeling change, without rewriting anything and without leaving Titus. That turns the isolation decision into a reversible setting, which is the opposite of the one-way door between Titus and EC2 that teams used to face. A team can try single tenancy for a quarter, measure it, and step back if the trade-off isn’t worth it for them.
What does not change is the contract. The Compute/Platform team still selects the instance type, patches the host, and sizes and scales the fleet underneath. The application team still uses the Titus API, the same delivery pipeline, and the same observability. Single tenancy is a new point on the isolation axis offered within the existing managed experience, not a separate product that the team has to learn and operate.
When a dedicated node is the wrong call
A dedicated node is a real cost, and single tenancy is not free isolation. Two things are worth weighing before reaching for it.
First, a single-tenant task does not get the whole machine; it gets the machine minus overhead. Every Titus container host, dedicated or shared, runs the platform sidecars, system services, the kubelet, and the host environment itself, and that overhead is a roughly fixed slice of CPU and a few gigabytes of memory. On a shared host, that slice is paid once and amortized across the many tasks running there. On a dedicated node, a single task handles it. Because the cost is fixed rather than proportional, it is punishing as a fraction of a small instance and negligible on a large one: a small dedicated node can lose tens of percent of its resources to overhead, while on the largest shapes it rounds to a couple of percent.
Second, because a task is placed on the smallest instance that fits it, there is usually a gap between what the task asked for and the next available shape, and on a dedicated node, that gap is pure waste, with no neighbors to soak it up. The two effects compound: fixed overhead plus the best-fit remainder set a ceiling on how much of a dedicated node a workload can actually use, and that ceiling is lowest exactly where people are tempted to reach for isolation casually, on small instances. However, this sizing waste can be reduced through coordination with the service owner as needed.
The guidance follows from the arithmetic. Single tenancy pays off for large, long-running, performance-sensitive, disruption-sensitive workloads, sized close to a node shape and run as fewer, larger replicas rather than many small ones. It is the wrong call for small, bursty, or highly elastic workloads, where the overhead fraction is high, the dedicated node sits mostly idle, and multi-tenant packing is both cheaper and faster to scale. This is also why the mode is allowlisted rather than a self-serve checkbox: the platform can keep workloads on the side of that line where they belong, and leave the ones that would gain little from a node of their own on the shared fleet, where they are cheaper to run.
Who’s using it
The first adopters are the workloads that motivated the work: real-time data infrastructure. Managed Apache Flink stream processing, streaming data connectors, and telemetry and logging pipelines were both the most frequent sources of network contention and the most damaged by it, because their recovery is expensive and their disruption budgets are tight. These are stateful, high-throughput jobs where a few seconds of starvation can cascade into minutes of catch-up, and where the platform’s own repacking used to be a source of disruption in its own right.
Moving them onto dedicated nodes removed the class of problem rather than mitigating it. The teams running them report stable operation, having previously seen intermittent, hard-to-attribute interference, and their jobs are no longer relocated by fleet repacking, removing a second, self-inflicted source of disruption. Latency-sensitive serving paths and a handful of GraphQL and edge services have followed for the same reason: a predictable tail matters more to them than a few points of bin-packing efficiency.
This is an ongoing rollout, not a finished one. We are widening the set of eligible workloads as we learn, using the largest production jobs as the stress test for the platform’s scaling assumptions, and watching the control-plane and EC2 launch-rate metrics as the count of small nodes grows. We have also been running periodic stress tests to exercise scaling ahead of real user workload, and making improvements to autoscaling and scheduling logic along the way.
What’s next
We are not done on either side of the tradeoff. On single tenancy, we are reducing launch latency with smarter pre-warming of common shapes, broadening the allowlist as scaling data holds up, and extending the model beyond long-running services as cost attribution and capacity stories mature. On the multi-tenant side, which remains the right default for most workloads, we are addressing the dimensions that hurt the most. The largest is the network: replacing HTB’s global-lock shaping with an eBPF-based Expected Departure Time approach that rate-limits by timestamping packets rather than contending on a lock, and pairing it with a lower-overhead container network device. We are also evaluating hardware cache and memory-bandwidth partitioning (Intel RDT and AMD PQoS) to give the kernel a real lever on the last-level cache, hardware GPU partitioning (NVIDIA MIG) for accelerator isolation, and continued work on the cgroup v2 IO controller for disk. This isolation benchmark lets us rank these by return on effort rather than by intuition, and show customers, in the numbers, that the shared fleet is getting quieter over time.
Single-tenant Titus is also a step toward something larger. Netflix’s Platform teams offer two ways to get compute: virtual machines on EC2 & containers on Titus. We want to replace that with a single Compute API that takes intent rather than mechanism into account: how much isolation a workload needs, how quickly it must launch, how long it can run without disruption, and what business domain it belongs to. The platform then makes placement and runtime choices, and can make globally optimal ones because it sees the whole picture.
Conclusion
Multi-tenancy is the right default for a container platform, and we will keep making it better for everyone. But the right default is not right for everything. Single-tenant Titus gives the workloads that need it the isolation of a dedicated VM, provisioned and patched by our existing node management, under the same API and the same managed experience, without taking away the freedom to change their mind. We can now point to the difference rather than describe it: a tail that stops moving under a noisy neighbor, a fleet that packs more densely once spreading is retired, and hosts that are faster and safer to patch. For the streaming and data systems at the heart of Netflix’s real-time platform, a room of one’s own turned out to be the feature that mattered.

Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

posts.title: AI on Your Terms: How We See AI in YouTrack
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
AI on your terms
When we published our YouTrack roadmap at the beginning of the year, we only briefly touched on our plans for AI. Now it’s time to share more details about how we see its role within YouTrack. 
Most project management tools now ship with AI built in and switched on by default. We’ve taken a different path. You decide whether AI belongs in your workflow, and if it does, which tools you want to use. Some teams run coding agents against their backlog all day. Others have strict policies and keep AI out completely. YouTrack is built to work well for both approaches.
With YouTrack, you choose whether and how to use AI, while we also make it easier to work with the tools you already trust. In this post, we explore the three options YouTrack gives you: connect your existing tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), use the built-in YouTrack AI Assistant, or keep AI switched off. We’ll also preview Ask YouTrack, an agentic AI chat we’re releasing later this year.
With any of these approaches, you get the same projects, Knowledge Base, and Helpdesk on Server or Cloud. This makes YouTrack an affordable alternative to the Atlassian stack and other AI-first solutions.
AI is becoming the default. With YouTrack, it remains your choice
Atlassian, monday.com, ClickUp, and other project management vendors are steadily expanding the role of AI in their products. Many of the teams we talk to aren’t completely ready for this shift, and their reasons vary. For some, it’s the effect on pricing; for others, it’s features they don’t need or unanswered questions about how their data is used in AI services. 
When we discuss migration from Atlassian with customers, their main concerns are the announced end of Data Center support and Atlassian’s updated data contribution practices. Effective August 17, 2026, de-identified and aggregated customer data may be used to improve Atlassian’s AI experiences, with opt-out options varying by plan.
YouTrack puts AI on your terms. If you switch it on, there are three ways to use it:
Connect your preferred AI chats, coding agents, automation platforms, IDEs, and workplace apps through YouTrack’s remote MCP server.
Enable our built-in AI Assistant to turn selected text into tasks, summarize content, get reply suggestions, improve your writing, and more.
Coming soon: Ask YouTrack, an agentic AI chat that understands your work. Search in YouTrack with prompts, get answers, create tasks, and propose updates – all within the chat and based on your project context. We also plan to let you bring your own key and use the LLM of your choice.
If you keep AI switched off, you still get YouTrack’s complete project management functionality, with nothing hidden behind AI features.
Option 1. Connect your AI stack to YouTrack through MCP
You can work with YouTrack from the AI applications and services your teams already use. The remote MCP server gives compatible tools access to the current YouTrack context while respecting each user’s existing permissions.
Choose from a variety of tools
AI chats – ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and others
Search and summarize tasks, support tickets, and Knowledge Base articles, or create and update work directly from an AI conversation. 
For example, you can easily connect YouTrack to Claude and search your project context using whatever details you have. If you’re a QA engineer managing multiplatform testing tasks, you can ask Claude to find unresolved tasks for testing on desktop, review them, and create a related task for similar testing on mobile devices in the same chat.




Coding agents and IDEs – PyCharm, IntelliJ IDEA, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and others
Give agents the YouTrack context they need, so they can find related documentation and reflect development progress in tasks, all without leaving your coding environment. For example, when implementing a new product feature, developers can ask Claude Code directly in IntelliJ IDEA to create the subtasks they need to tackle next.




Delegating task management to coding agents is becoming a common practice, and for such teams, YouTrack evolves from automating individual processes to serving as a shared “agentic database” for agent and human-led tasks.
The Fullworks case study shows how a software company supporting 12 products, including Broadcaster, a messaging platform for UK trade businesses, has integrated agents throughout its software development lifecycle. The team connects Claude Code to YouTrack through MCP to manage development work directly from its coding tools. Its agents create and update tasks, verify release requirements, and help coordinate development across its products.



    
Read the Fullworks case study
                                    
Automation platforms – n8n, Zapier, Make, OpenAI AgentKit, and others
If you rely on process automation on a platform of your choice, as a part of it, you can build agentic workflows that route requests, create and update tasks, log time, and trigger actions in YouTrack. Marketing teams, for example, can use the n8n integration to automatically turn budget requests submitted through a form into YouTrack tasks.




Beyond this example, you can integrate YouTrack into every step of your automation to update work items in response to actions from AI agents, share YouTrack content with other systems, and support a wide range of cross-tool workflows.
Workplace tools – service desks, internal portals, custom applications, and others
Your teams can work with project information through organization-level apps or internal AI assistants. You can add custom MCP actions with YouTrack apps or build automation using workflows and API-based scripts – in-house or with help from one of the YouTrack consulting partners.
This approach can scale to meet the needs of large enterprise customers. For example, Gurtam develops telematics and IoT platforms for B2B customers and operates in more than 160 countries. The team connected its internal AI platform, Nova, to YouTrack MCP. Managers and employees now use AI agents to create structured tasks, review feature requests, monitor backlogs, prepare changelogs, and turn meeting notes into actionable work.



    
Read the Gurtam case study
                                    
Choose the right connection method
How you connect depends on what the tool supports. YouTrack supports OAuth authorization for compatible MCP clients, so users do not need to create or store permanent tokens. OAuth works with browser-based, desktop, and mobile AI applications, as well as shared organization-level services. You can also add YouTrack directly from the ChatGPT or Claude connector directory and set it up company-wide. The connection is available for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, and Edu workspaces.
Simplify setup with CIMD
If an MCP client supports CIMD, a YouTrack administrator can allow it to register automatically. This removes most of the manual configuration and makes approved tools easier to connect.
Register an OAuth client manually
Manual registration is required when an application supports OAuth but not CIMD. This may apply to custom internal applications or AI clients that cannot register automatically.
Use a permanent token as a fallback
For local agents, custom scripts, and other tools without OAuth support, permanent-token authorization remains available. Tokens should be stored securely and are best suited to controlled local or custom integrations.
Learn how to connect AI tools
                                    
Option 2. Enhance efficiency with built-in AI assistance
The second option is our built-in AI Assistant that can handle routine work across YouTrack. Administrators have the option to manage access or disable AI entirely. Your data remains yours and is never used to train AI models, whether you choose YouTrack Cloud or Server.
Currently, AI Assistant includes a limited number of free credits, replenished weekly. It is available to YouTrack Cloud customers, including teams on the free plan, and to YouTrack Server customers using the free plan or an active paid subscription.
When Ask YouTrack and BYOK are introduced in Q4 2026, AI access will change:
Free AI Assistant credits will be included only with paid YouTrack Cloud plans.
Paid credits will be available through a connected JetBrains AI subscription to YouTrack Cloud and Server customers on free plans or with active paid subscriptions.
BYOK will also be available to YouTrack Cloud and Server customers on free plans or with active paid subscriptions.




Text-to-issue transformation
Scan selected text for action items, choose which ones to turn into tasks, and create them together.
Writing assistance
Check grammar, spelling, and punctuation in tasks, articles, support tickets, and comments. Get phrase suggestions while writing in English or German. 
The built-in YouTrack writing assistant is powered by JetBrains AI and will continue to run exclusively on JetBrains infrastructure.
Effortless summaries with AI
Generate concise summaries of project tasks, articles, and support tickets, regardless of the discussion length or language.
Reply suggestions
Generate context-aware replies, including general responses, apologies, or requests for more time. Use the suggested text as written or edit it before posting.
Text recognition from images
Extract editable and searchable text from screenshots, document photos, and other image attachments. YouTrack can also include images containing matching text in search results.
The text recognition feature doesn’t require a connection to external services. For YouTrack Cloud, processing takes place on JetBrains infrastructure, while for YouTrack Server, it runs within your local environment.
Discover YouTrack AI Assistance
                                    
Coming soon: Ask YouTrack and BYOK
Ask YouTrack, a built-in agentic AI chat, is planned for Q4 2026. It works with your current YouTrack context: Search through prompts, ask it about your projects, get answers in chat, understand the state of work, create tasks, and propose updates for your review.
We plan to add BYOK (Bring Your Own Key) support, so you can connect your own AI providers and use the LLM of your choice – in line with your company’s policies and budget.




Coming soon: Task creation from Slack threads
For teams that use Slack for everyday collaboration, we also plan to add a new AI-powered feature available in the YouTrack Slack app in Q4 2026 that lets you create a task from a thread. You’ll be able to automatically turn a conversation in your team channel into a task, or add instructions along the way to specify what it should include.




Option 3. Experience high-quality project management without AI
YouTrack’s core functionality does not depend on AI. Administrators can disable AI features entirely. Teams with strict AI policies can plan projects, track tasks on Agile boards and Gantt charts, maintain documentation in the Knowledge Base, and manage customer or internal requests in Helpdesk – all without AI anywhere in their workflow.
Server or Cloud – your choice!
For greater control over your infrastructure and data, you can choose YouTrack Server. It scales to hundreds of thousands of users, supports GDPR and SOC 2 compliance, integrates with existing identity systems, and provides real-time monitoring. 
YouTrack Cloud is hosted and maintained by JetBrains, with a choice of AWS regions in Northern California, Frankfurt, Ireland, and Singapore. Both versions offer the same functionality, with AI on your terms, whichever you choose.
Save up to 70% compared with Jira and Confluence
Whether or not you enable AI, YouTrack’s total cost of ownership can be up to 70% lower than Jira and Confluence combined, and that’s before Atlassian’s service management and plugin costs are added.
YouTrack is free for a team of up to 10 users. YouTrack Server subscriptions start at \$900 per year for 15 users, while YouTrack Cloud starts at \$4.50 per user per month for teams of 11 or more users.
YouTrack Helpdesk includes three support agents and unlimited reporters for free. Additional agents cost \$6 per agent per month.
If you have any other questions about AI in YouTrack or migration, please share them in the comments below or get in touch with our technical support. We’re always here to help.
Your YouTrack team
AI or no AI, Server or Cloud – you choose!

posts.title: Busy Plugin Developers Newsletter – Q3 2026
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Your quarterly dose of plugin dev news, tools, and tips from JetBrains
⚡JetBrains Plugin Developer Conf 2026 Is Coming!
November 10, 2026 | Online | Free
Join our annual free virtual event on developing plugins for JetBrains products. You’ll hear talks from SAP, Broadcom, JetBrains experts, and independent plugin authors.
Register Now
                                    
🤖 AI meets plugins: ACP and MCP integrations, plus where AI-assisted development helps – and where it doesn’t.
⚙️IntelliJ Platform updates: The latest Gradle Plugin, Plugin DevKit, Plugin Verifier, and API updates.
💻 Real-world techniques: LSP, WSL, Dev Containers, web-based UIs, and plugin architectures that scale. 




🧩 Marketplace Updates
New Way to Edit Plugin Description 
Keeping your plugin page up to date just got easier! You can now edit your plugin description directly on the plugin’s page. The description is stored separately from the plugin archive, so you can update it without uploading a new plugin version. Learn more  →
UI Freeze Reports Are Now Available in the Freezes Tab
Users say the IDE froze, but you can’t reproduce it? JetBrains Marketplace now collects UI freeze reports for your plugin, with full thread dumps and CPU snapshots. In his guide, Jakub Chrzanowski explains how to read the reports, enable reporting, and use an AI agent to find the cause. You can also watch his video or see the Marketplace documentation →.




🔧 Plugin Development Tooling Updates
IntelliJ Plugin Verifier 1.411
Tool that checks binary compatibility between IntelliJ-based IDE builds and plugins. 
Content modules are now supported in dependency resolution, dependency trees, and module visibility checks, and dependencies.txt lists each plugin’s content modules.
New public APIs for plugin name validation, rebuilding dependencies, and keeping only direct dependencies in verification results.
Lower memory usage for check-trunk-api and report generation, which now streams dependencies.txt and HTML reports.
Reports are now written in UTF-8.
Updated Gradle, Bouncy Castle, and Byte Buddy.
View Changelog →
IntelliJ Platform Gradle Plugin 2.19.0
Plugin that helps configure your environment for building, testing, verifying, and publishing plugins for IntelliJ-based IDEs. 
New buildPluginVariants tasks build Linux, macOS, and Windows plugin distributions for x86_64 and arm64 (2026.1+).
New testFrameworks() helper, more test framework options, and per-plugin bundled-library exclusions.
Full --offline support, and Kotlin stdlib and Coroutines are no longer bundled into the sandbox by default.
verifyPlugin now runs against each IDE’s own bundled JBR and fails based on report files.
Removed the deprecated setupDependencies task (breaking change), and tasks are now organized into separate groups.
Plus fixes for download URL resolution, signature verification, and cache writes.
View Changelog →
💡 Tip of the Quarter
Use Release Channels for Pre-releases
Deploy plugins to non-default release channels (alpha, beta, canary, eap) to share work-in-progress with limited user groups and gather feedback before public release. This lets you test with real users without affecting your main release.
📚 Resources & Learning
📖 Blog
IDE Plugin Generator – The New Beginning
Creating an IntelliJ Platform plugin no longer means choosing between the IDE wizard and the GitHub template. The new web-based generator combines both, with dependency selection, GitHub workflows, and Split Mode support, all from the IDE or your browser. Find out why we made the change and what’s coming next. Read →
The Evolution of WSL Support in JetBrains IDEs
After trying three other approaches, JetBrains IDEs now open WSL projects in Native mode, up to 38% faster. Learn how the IJent agent and EelApi make this work, and how your plugin can run the same way in WSL, Docker, and Dev Containers. Read →
Why We Still Need an IDE
Agents write the code, but someone still has to steer, verify, and own it. Read why the IDE is becoming the cockpit for agentic development, and why its tools matter as much to agents as they do to developers. Read →




⭐ Community Spotlight
Native Calls in IntelliJ Platform Plugins: JNA vs FFM
The IntelliJ Platform is moving native integrations from JNA to Java’s Foreign Function and Memory API. In this video, Patrick Scheibe shows how to configure the IDE-bundled JNA, when your existing code can stay, and how to start with FFM if your plugin calls native code.






Save State in IntelliJ Plugins in 3 Lines!
Need your plugin to remember a setting after an IDE restart? In this short video, Róbert Novotný shows how to save booleans, numbers, strings, and string lists with PropertiesComponent in just three lines of Kotlin.






💌 Until next time — happy plugin development!
JetBrains Marketplace team

posts.title: JetBrains GameDev Day 2026: Watch the Recordings
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Missed JetBrains GameDev Day 2026, or want to revisit your favorite sessions? All the recordings are now available on YouTube!
On September 28, we brought together game developers, engineers, and industry experts for a full day of technical talks, live demos, and discussions about the tools and challenges shaping modern game development.
From Epic’s open-source Lore VCS and ECS in a live game to Unreal Engine profiling, Unity UI automation, AI-driven PCG in Godot, and debugging across C# and C++, this year’s sessions stayed close to real production problems.
Whether you joined us online, attended one of our watch parties in Belgrade or Limassol, or couldn’t make it this time, you can now catch up on everything at your own pace.
Watch the full JetBrains GameDev Day 2026 playlist on YouTube
Watch the sessions
Not sure where to start? Pick your engine or role:
Unreal Engine: Death by a Thousand Ticks and Agentic Development in Unreal Engine with JetBrains Rider
Unity: Fix Your CI Without Leaving the IDE and How We Automated Figma-to-Unity UI Integration With AI Agents
Godot: Prompt to Playable World
Engine and backend programmers: Evolving a Live Game Engine and Debugging Across Two Runtimes and Two Different Languages
Build, pipelines, and infrastructure: Splitting the Difference and Code Quality Never Changes
Everyone, especially leads and juniors: Pass the Controller?
Pass the Controller? Communities, Data, and AI in Game Development
Anthony Tešija (Discord), Jason Weimann (Boddle Learning), Gennadii Potapov (General Arcade), and Anton Licht (Sudden Forest)
Moderated by Denis Savosin (JetBrains)
Our opening panel explored the role of communities, data, and AI in game development. When should developers listen to community feedback, and when is it better to trust their own vision? How can AI support developers without replacing critical thinking, especially for those just entering the industry?
Fix Your CI Without Leaving the IDE: TeamCity MCP and CLI (with Unity)
Artem Rokhin (JetBrains)
Discover how TeamCity’s MCP support and CLI bring continuous integration workflows directly into your development environment. Using a Unity project as an example, Artem demonstrated how to investigate build failures and interact with CI pipelines without constantly switching between tools.
Learn more: TeamCity MCP and CLI for AI agents
Evolving a Live Game Engine: Introducing ECS Without a Full Rewrite
Alex Zhorau (Meta)
How do you bring an Entity Component System into a mass-market game that’s already live without rewriting the engine? Drawing on proprietary engines and Unreal Engine, Alex walked through a staged migration, the compromises around memory layout and scripting, and why a hybrid of ECS and legacy code is often where a live game should end up, not just a stop along the way.
Code Quality Never Changes: How Static Analysis Can Help in the Age of AI
Kai Schmithusen (JetBrains)
AI-generated code brings new productivity opportunities, but also new challenges for code quality. Learn how static analysis can help teams identify issues, manage technical debt, and maintain reliable development workflows, with practical examples using Qodana.
Learn more: Qodana
Prompt to Playable World: Live-Building AI-Driven PCG with Godot, C#, and Gemini
Sharmishtha Sen (Jet Heart Labs)
Watch a procedural world generation pipeline come together using Godot, C#, and AI. Sharmishtha demonstrated how to turn natural-language prompts into playable environments while combining AI-generated configurations with traditional procedural generation techniques and Rider’s development tools.
Learn more: Godot support in JetBrains Rider
Death by a Thousand Ticks: Why Gameplay Systems Become Slow
Konrad Słoń (Fool’s Theory)
Performance problems rarely appear overnight. Through Unreal Engine examples and live profiling, Konrad explored how small engineering decisions accumulate into gameplay bottlenecks and demonstrated practical optimization workflows using Unreal Insights and Rider.
How We Automated Figma-to-Unity UI Integration With AI Agents
Alina Chupakhina (Playkot) and Olia Chupakhina (Cubic Games)
Alina and Olia shared a Figma-to-Unity pipeline that grew over years of production and now runs through an AI agent over MCP. They covered the design foundation that makes automation possible, the lessons learned from building it, and a benchmark of which UI integration tasks the agent can handle today and which still need a human.
Agentic Development in Unreal Engine with JetBrains Rider
Alexander Dzerakh (JetBrains)
Go beyond AI-assisted code generation with agentic workflows tailored to Unreal Engine. Through live demos, Alexander showed how Rider, ACP, and Unreal Engine-specific skills can help AI agents navigate engine architecture, generate C++ code, investigate crashes, and automate development tasks.
Learn more: AI agent skills for Unreal Engine in Rider
Splitting the Difference: How Epic’s Lore VCS Handles Massive Binary Files
Ben Cooke and Ryn Slack (AWS)
Most version control systems were built for code, not multi-gigabyte assets that change every day. Ben and Ryn explained how Epic Games’ open-source Lore VCS splits files into content-addressable fragments so only the changed part of an asset moves, why its edge caches can fill on demand instead of being pre-seeded, and how to deploy it yourself with the Lore module in the AWS Cloud Game Development Toolkit.
Learn more: Lore on GitHub · Lore documentation · AWS Cloud Game Development Toolkit
Debugging Across Two Runtimes and Two Different Languages
Alex Drum (Hytale)
Your client is C#, your server is C++, and the bug lives somewhere in between. Alex showed how to debug both runtimes at once with Rider and CLion, read the data crossing the protocol, and figure out which runtime is lying, and discussed why the boundary between them is the last place to look, not the first.
Keep learning and building
A huge thank you to all our speakers, hosts, and everyone who joined us online or at our watch parties in Belgrade and Limassol! Special thanks to DevGAMM x FTW! for co-hosting our Belgrade watch party. We hope these sessions give you new ideas, useful techniques, and inspiration for your own projects.
Watch all JetBrains GameDev Day 2026 recordings on YouTube
If you’d like to explore the tools featured throughout the event, check out JetBrains tools for game development.
Many of the demos ran in JetBrains Rider, which is free for non-commercial use, including learning, pet projects, and open-source contributions.
To hear about the next GameDev Day first, subscribe to the JetBrains GameDev newsletter.
See you at the next GameDev Day!

posts.title: Air Governance: Manage AI Agents, Access, and Spend Throughout Your Organization
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Today, JetBrains Air Governance becomes generally available. Formerly known as JetBrains Central, this is the organization layer of JetBrains Air, a system of products for agentic development. Air Governance gives you one place to manage which AI agents, models, and providers your teams use, set spending limits, and see what that usage costs and delivers. It works with Claude Agent, Codex, Gemini CLI, Junie, and other ACP-compatible agents, across various developer surfaces, including IDEs, the CLI, web browsers, and mobile.
Air Governance is now available to all JetBrains organizational customers, with both free and paid plans available to meet the needs of diverse teams.






Why we built Air Governance
Most engineering teams now use several AI tools from different providers at the same time. They work with AI agents via an IDE, CLI, or web interface, and they switch between Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Junie, and others. Because each tool comes with its own contract, dashboard, and admin settings, it’s hard to get the full picture of who uses which agents and models, how much AI is costing the company, and whether it is actually helping.
We had the same problem at JetBrains. Our AI spend grew roughly tenfold in the first half of 2026, and our first cross-vendor usage report took four days to compile by hand. We built a suite of tools to address this problem, and those tools became Air Governance, which now helps manage the agentic usage of roughly 2,300 people at JetBrains every month. 
Air Governance allows admins to manage AI usage through one console. It works across vendors, which means developers can use the agents and models that fit their tasks. When a new agent or model comes out, you can simply add it to the same policies. There is no new contract or separate admin setup.
Managing AI throughout your organization
In the console, you can:
Set AI credit limits for individual users, teams, and service accounts, so budgets are enforced rather than just reported.









Manage AI providers and set up centralized BYOK: Use JetBrains AI, or connect your own OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, or Google Vertex AI accounts.









Define which AI agents are approved for use throughout the organization.









Configure MCP servers at the company level, so everyone works with the same approved external tools.









Create AI policies that combine approved providers, models, agents, and credit limits for different groups of users. 
Track your costs and what they deliver
Spending more on AI is easy. Explaining to leadership what that spend delivers is much harder. Air Governance allows you to track both cost and impact across all your agents:
AI costs by user: See where your budget goes, down to each developer. 









AI costs by agent: Compare spend across Junie, Claude Agent, Codex, Gemini CLI, and other agents.





AI costs by model and provider: Understand which models drive your bill. 









AI outcome metrics: See how AI is changing how your developers work. Metrics include the split between human-authored and AI-generated code, as well as how much code is AI-generated or AI-modified.








For details on how each metric is calculated, see the AI analytics documentation.  
What’s next
Air will evolve through a series of releases, and Air Governance will follow the same approach. Here are some of the capabilities we’re working on:
MCP server propagation to third-party CLIs, so company-approved tools reach every agent, not just JetBrains ones.
GitHub Copilot support through Air Gateway, our connector for third-party CLIs.
Connections to cloud agents through Air Gateway.
Advanced AI analytics.
Credit limits and custom pricing for BYOK models.
The ability to manage skills across teams.
Get started with Air Governance
Air Governance is now available for all organizations as part of the Business plan, which costs USD 20 per month for each developer with AI access. Developers don’t need individual AI licenses, and they draw on a shared pool of AI credits, which your organization buys separately and which cover AI usage across JetBrains products and connected agents.
Request a Demo
                                    
Existing JetBrains customers can explore Air Governance directly in the console (admin access required).
Join the webinar: see Air Governance in action on November 18, 4:00–5:00 PM CET. Our product team will walk you through access and usage policies, spending limits, costs and usage analytics, and answer your questions live. 
Register for the webinar

posts.title: Small Talk with Ulises Olave, CTO and Co-Founder of Fitia
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
What is Small Talk?
Small Talk is our short Q&A with founders from the JetBrains Startup Program. They answer a handful of questions in their own words about what they’re building, why they started, and what they’ve figured out along the way. No pitch, no polish – just a two-minute read to meet the person behind the product.
This time, we’re talking to Ulises Olave, CTO and Co-Founder of Fitia, a nutrition app that has grown to 10 million+ users in Latin America and beyond. He shares how his team brought four kinds of databases together in one place, why the rapid advancement of AI made JetBrains the first company his team went to for help, and how a small engineering team achieved a pace of one major feature per month.
Ulises Olave, CTO and Co-Founder of Fitia
Fitia is an AI-powered meal planning and calorie tracking app. Founded in Peru in 2019 by Piero Linares and Ulises Olave and backed by Y Combinator (Summer 2021), it’s the top nutrition app in Latin America and is now scaling in the US. Fitia joined the JetBrains Startup Program to help their lean team ship even faster by bringing DataGrip and GoLand into their workflow.
TL;DR
Fitia’s AI coach processes more than 30 million food logs a month, alongside data on weight, sleep, steps, and water. As the product has evolved, this data has been spread across different database types and providers.
DataGrip has given Fitia’s team one central place to work with all their databases, including PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Azure, and Redis. Its built-in AI features have also helped the team cut query times from hours down to mere seconds.
GoLand has helped Fitia roughly double their development speed on its Go microservices. They now ship three times faster than before, at a rate of one major feature per month.
What is Fitia, for someone who’s never used it?
Fitia is a meal-planning and calorie-tracking app. You tell it your goal – whether that’s losing weight or gaining muscle – and it builds a personalized plan that adapts to your data, your progress, and the foods you actually like to eat. The engine behind this is our own AI coach. We’re the top nutrition app in Latin America, and this year the goal is to become a leading health and fitness app in the US, too.
What was the biggest challenge you faced as Fitia grew?
Data. We store food records for all our users. This means more than 30 million items logged every month, plus data on weight, sleep, steps, and water intake. As our data grew, it ended up spread across several different database types and providers, and keeping integrity across all of them became a challenge. Even a simple query became a real headache in that kind of fragmented setup.
How did you deal with that?
We centralized everything in one place. We pulled our PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Azure, and Redis databases into DataGrip, so instead of jumping between providers, we could work with all our data in a single tool. And after centralizing it, we’ve been able to leverage DataGrip’s built-in AI as well. The query suggestions cut work that used to take hours down to seconds, especially against those complex multi-provider setups.
Why JetBrains?
We’d been using JetBrains tools from early on, so when AI started advancing at an almost absurd pace, JetBrains was the first company we turned to. Every month one of the big providers would release a better model, which meant we could suddenly deliver more features, and faster. We needed every developer to be fast enough to ship powerful features every month without expanding the team, and we needed one tool that covered the whole path, from writing the code to deploying it. We applied to the Startup Program, got accepted in a few days, and within a week the team was using DataGrip and GoLand daily.
Was there anything that surprised you?
How well integrated the AI is. At first, we were just focused on getting more efficient with solid IDEs. We didn’t expect the AI to be built in so natively. The context-aware chat lets you ask questions right inside the IDE, using your own code as context, and that changed how we worked more than we thought it would.
What specific impact has GoLand had?
With GoLand, we roughly doubled our development speed for our Go microservices. The code suggestions and optimization tooling let us build and deploy faster, which means our mobile team can rely on clean, reliable backend services and ship features much faster. The product goal is one major feature every month. That used to take us about three times as long. This year we’ve been holding that pace consistently.
Where does Fitia go from here?
AI has opened up possibilities in nutrition that were almost unimaginable before, from identifying food in a photo to reading a user’s data and giving personalized recommendations. Our strategy isn’t to compete with the big model providers – it’s to build on top of them, using their capabilities while training on our own community data, so we can create features that actually mean something to our users. Beyond that, we’ll just keep focusing on developer efficiency, because that’s what lets a small team move like a big one.




Read the full case study here.
JetBrains Startup Program FAQ
Q: Do I qualify?
A: You qualify if your company is privately owned, established within the last five years, and has a website or other discoverable online presence.
Q: Where do I apply?
A: You can apply here.
Q: What is the timeline for the JetBrains Startup Program application process?
A: After you apply, our team will review your application within 48 hours. If you meet the criteria, you will receive an acceptance email, followed by a quote for the products. If you’re not accepted, our team will get in touch and share our reasoning. An application may be unsuccessful either due to missing information (e.g., a document or website) or because you do not meet our eligibility requirements (e.g., your business is more than five years old).
Q: What products are included in the terms “IDE subscription” and “team or learning tool subscription”?
A: A variety of products are available through IDE subscriptions, including IDEs as well as .NET and Visual Studio tools. “Team tool subscription” refers to team tools, including TeamCity, YouTrack, Datalore, Qodana, and our learning tool (JetBrains Academy).
